Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Architect
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Feeling Ill: Feeling physically unwell, Auditory (Language Confusion): Incomprehensible chatter, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted

Vignette:
Rajan Mehta is a 41-year-old South Asian architect who presented for treatment following a period of escalating distress that he described, with some difficulty, as having "finally become impossible to manage alone." He is married, and it was his wife who first noticed that the man she had known for over a decade had become someone she no longer fully recognized — withdrawn, rigid in his routines, and prone to sudden, inexplicable alarm. What Rajan had not told her, until very recently, was that the source of his distress predated their marriage by several years, rooted in a relationship he had spent a long time trying to bury in professional achievement and deliberate silence.

In his early thirties, Rajan was involved with a woman he had met through a mutual social circle. The relationship was volatile in ways he had initially attributed to passion, then to stress, and finally to something he could not name without implicating himself in a story he found deeply shameful. She drank heavily, and when she drank, the apartment they shared would fill with a particular quality of noise — slurred, looping speech that collapsed into something almost phonemic, words losing their edges, her voice cycling through registers he could no longer parse. On several occasions, during these episodes, she became physically violent. The worst incident occurred on a winter evening when Rajan had come home unwell, feverish and nauseated, and had lain down on the couch. He had not heard her come in. He had not processed, in any sequential way, what happened next — only that his body had understood before his mind did, the shadow crossing the room, the shift in air pressure, and then impact. He remembered it now not as a continuous event but as a series of arrested frames: the grain of the couch fabric against his cheek, the smell of alcohol very close to his face, a particular angle of lamplight, the ceiling. Still photographs. Each one carrying the full emotional weight of the original moment, so that to remember any one of them was, for Rajan, not recollection but re-entry.

He ended the relationship within months of that night and told no one. He built his career with considerable discipline, joined a respected firm, married a woman he loved and trusted, and understood himself, for a time, to have moved on. The first sign that this was not true came at an office gathering where a colleague spilled wine nearby and the smell reached him before the sound of breaking glass did. His body had already moved — chair pushed back, hands braced — before he had any conscious thought. He stood there, heart hammering, in a room full of colleagues, and had no explanation to offer anyone, including himself.

In his work as an architect, Rajan regularly attends client consultations and site meetings, environments where overlapping conversations are common. When multiple voices blur into simultaneous, unintelligible sound — the particular acoustic texture of a crowded conference room — he finds himself scanning the space with an alertness disproportionate to any identifiable threat. He sleeps poorly, lying awake in a state of readiness he cannot entirely account for, as though some part of him has not accepted that the night is safe. He startles at sounds his wife does not even register.

What has accumulated alongside these responses is a set of beliefs about himself that Rajan finds more distressing than the symptoms themselves. He had come to believe, with a quiet and persistent certainty, that he had failed in the most fundamental way a person could — that he had not protected himself, had not acted rightly, had not been the person he was supposed to be. He felt that the trust he had extended in that relationship had been turned against him in a way that still colored how he understood his own judgment. He was not sure, even now, that he could trust himself to respond correctly when it mattered.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment at his daughter's school, when a cluster of parents talking over one another in the hallway sent him out of the building and into the parking lot, where he sat in his car for twenty minutes unable to go back inside. He had missed the performance. His daughter had looked for him in the audience. He arrived for the last session of treatment hoping, above everything else, to be someone his family could count on — and afraid, in equal measure, that he had already proved he was not.
